Ashek Ahmad, directeur de la mosquée Kha: Ashek Ahmad, director of the Khadijah Mosque, and his son Anas.
À Pointe-Saint-Charles, les graffitis su: In Pointe-Saint-Charles, the graffiti on the façade is the first thing you notice when you stop in front of the English-language Khadijah Mosque.
Impossible de passer outre, tant ils att: They’re impossible to ignore, so much do they draw the eye with their sheer size. These modern hieroglyphs are practically illegible, and our team of budding journalists from La Converse quickly gives up on trying to decipher them and pushes open the front door. Inside, the atmosphere is completely different. Something solemn and spiritual hangs in the air. You would feel guilty fiddling with your phone in a place many consider sacred. The first thing we notice is that everyone greets us. “Aleykoum salam,” an older man says as he walks by. Does he think we’re all Muslim?
On découvrira bientôt que ce n’est pas l: We would soon find out that’s not the case. We take off our shoes, and Ashek Ahmad, the warm and welcoming director of the mosque, greets us graciously. Before long, our team is deep in conversation with him and Nafija Rahman, a well-known worshipper in the neighbourhood. Ashek Ahmad tells us about the situation at the mosque and the difficulties facing the surrounding communities, and he speaks to us about Islam. He also tells us the story of Khadijah, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, after whom the mosque is named. An entrepreneur, she could be a model of perseverance for many young girls, Ashek believes. “[…] She was the equivalent of a billionaire in those days,” adds Nafija Rahman.
Ashek Ahmad évoque l’insécurité alimenta: Ashek Ahmad speaks of the food insecurity many families in the neighbourhood and the community are facing. He feels the city offers little support in this regard. But whether they are mosques or churches, places of worship are becoming aid centres for many families in the area. During Ramadan, Ashek has taken it upon himself to distribute food to these families. “The hadith says we must make sure our neighbours, 40 neighbours to the north, east, south and west, are taken care of […],” Nafija explains.
Ainsi, pendant le mois du ramadan, Ashek: And so, during the month of Ramadan, Ashek helps 160 neighbours of all backgrounds, origins and religions – students, families newly settled in Canada, seniors, and more. Suddenly, it’s 7:50 p.m. It’s time for Iftar, the breaking of the fast. We’re invited to go eat, but first, we pray. While several members of the La Converse team are regulars at mosques, it’s a first for me. I join the worshippers, positioning myself at the very back.
Je ne connais pas les mots de la prière,: I don’t know the words of the prayer, but I mimic the movements of those next to me. We stand. We kneel. We press our foreheads to the floor. We stand again. We kneel. We press our foreheads to the floor. There is something therapeutic about repeating these movements; my mind empties of every thought and every outside concern. In that moment, nothing matters more than the present. I think of the worshippers at the Sainte-Foy mosque, and at the mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, who were doing the same thing when a terrorist walked into their place of prayer. Finally, we can eat. Everyone sits on the floor. We share the meal in good spirits and get to know a group of Pakistani students from Concordia.
« Ce n’est pas notre mosquée, nous appre: “This isn’t our mosque,” one of them tells us, laughing. “We come here for the food.” Everyone is welcome here, and the man who greeted me earlier knew I wasn’t Muslim, but it mattered little to him. The Khadijah Mosque opens its doors to everyone, Muslim and non-Muslim alike, and out of kindness offers each person the little it has. Outside, the graffiti is still there, giving off an ominous aura, the product of hateful, Islamophobic feelings. What were the people who vandalized the mosque thinking?
Nous, on n’y a trouvé que de la fraterni: All we found there was fraternity, love, deep respect for tradition, and a spirit of sharing. All you have to do is push open the door to discover the same thing.
